newsitem.title: USA: Egypt says Israel hurting peace prospects.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says Israel hurting peace prospects.

text.p: Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said on Monday that Israel's decision to build new housing for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem was a mistake that would dampen prospects for peace in the region.
Moussa said Egypt would support Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat if he follows through on a threat to unilaterally create an independent Palestinian state.

"Many governments commit mistakes, so it's one of those mistakes," Moussa told Reuters following a speech to a business group here. "The Israelis have to understand that playing politics at the expense of the peace process will only make things worse.
"We totally and without reservation oppose that (settlement) policy," he said.
Arafat on Saturday accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of trying to destroy the peace process by choosing to put up a 6,500-home Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem.
He warned he might declare an independent Palestinian state in response, which drew Moussa's support.

"Why not? They have to have a Palestinian state, there is no question about that. So if Yasser Arafat and the people of Palestine wish to do so, it is up to them to decide," Moussa said. "We'll just support what Arafat says."
Netanyahu has warned that Arafat would bring peace moves to a halt if he unilaterally declared a state now.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East War and views the entire city as its capital, but the Palestinians want East Jerusalem as capital of a future state.
Arafat, in Washington on Monday to meet with President Bill Clinton, said the Israeli settlements were aimed at isolating East Jerusalem and strengthening Israel's hold on the region.

The Israeli moves came just weeks before Israel and the Palestinians were due to resume talks on a permanent peace deal, which were to include negotiations on the future of Jerusalem. Clinton said on Monday the Israeli decision had put a cloud of "mistrust" over the peace process.
Despite current tensions, Moussa said a peace agreement was possible by a previously agreed-upon 1999 deadline "if everybody thinks in a statesman-like manner.
"We don't want to enter into the next century with the Palestinian question still hanging around," he said.
